properties.name: Athens
properties.one_line: An Indian king named Porus sent ambassadors to Augustus around 20 BCE, bearing tigers and a nine-cubit snake as gifts after a journey of several years. One envoy, the philosopher Zarmanochegas, burned himself alive in Athens, and Romans raised him a tomb inscribed with his name and home city of Bargosa. Strabo and Cassius Dio both recorded the embassy in detail.
properties.image_credit: Acropolis of Athens, where the Indian envoy Zarmanochegas died · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Charax Spasinu
properties.one_line: Han general Gan Ying reached the Persian Gulf coast in 97 CE on a mission to reach Rome, the farthest west any Chinese envoy had traveled. Parthian sailors warned him the sea crossing could take two years and cost his life, so he turned back without ever setting foot on Roman soil. His report still gave China its earliest detailed written account of the Roman Empire.
properties.image_credit: Shatt al-Arab waterway near the Persian Gulf coast Gan Ying reached in 97 CE · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Rhandeia
properties.one_line: Roman general Corbulo and the Parthian prince Tiridates met at Rhandeia in 63 CE and ended five years of war over Armenia's throne. Tiridates laid his diadem before a statue of Nero and agreed to receive his crown only from Roman hands afterward. The settlement held for about fifty years, until Trajan annexed Armenia outright in 114 CE.
properties.image_credit: The Euphrates River in eastern Turkey, near the historic Rhandeia region (representative image) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Parthian king Phraates IV sent four of his own sons to Rome around 10 BCE as hostages, cementing peace and letting Augustus boast of Parthia's submission in his Res Gestae. One son, Vonones, grew up in Rome and later returned east to briefly rule as Parthia's king before his Roman manners cost him the throne. Augustus displayed the arrangement as one of the great diplomatic triumphs of his reign.
properties.image_credit: Palatine Hill, Rome, seat of the imperial household that hosted foreign princes · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Nero crowned the Parthian prince Tiridates king of Armenia in the Roman Forum in 66 CE, closing out years of war with a public spectacle. Tiridates arrived after a nine-month overland journey with 3,000 horsemen rather than cross the sea, and Nero replaced his tiara with a Roman diadem before a cheering crowd. Trajan ended the arrangement by annexing Armenia outright in 114 CE.
properties.image_credit: The Roman Forum, site of Tiridates I's coronation by Nero in 66 CE · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ravenna
properties.one_line: Thumelicus, the young son of the Germanic chieftain Arminius, was paraded as a three-year-old captive in Germanicus's Roman triumph of 17 CE and then sent to live out his life in exile at Ravenna. His father had destroyed three Roman legions at the Teutoburg Forest less than a decade before. Ancient sources leave his later years obscure, recording only that he never returned to Germania.
properties.image_credit: Fragments of Ravenna's Porta Aurea, built in 42 CE during Thumelicus's lifetime there · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Zeugma
properties.one_line: Augustus's grandson Gaius Caesar met the Parthian king Phraates V on an island in the Euphrates in 2 CE, each bringing an equal armed escort to the meeting. The two feasted together afterward and confirmed the river as the boundary between their empires, recognizing Parthia as Rome's sovereign equal for the first time in decades. The peace this summit secured lasted through the rest of Augustus's reign.
properties.image_credit: The Euphrates River near the Roman-Parthian frontier crossing at Zeugma (representative image) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Muziris
properties.one_line: Roman ships sailed directly to the Indian port of Muziris on the monsoon winds, a route the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea described in detail around 40 to 70 CE. A surviving papyrus contract records a single ship's cargo of pepper and ivory valued at nearly 7 million sesterces. Pliny the Elder complained this eastern trade drained 50 million sesterces a year out of the Roman economy.
properties.image_credit: Pattanam Excavation Museum, near the site of ancient Muziris · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Arikamedu
properties.one_line: Roman merchants established a trading settlement at Arikamedu on India's Coromandel coast, where archaeologists later excavated Italian wine amphorae and Arretine tableware stamped with Roman potters' names. British archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler's 1945 excavation confirmed direct Roman contact continuing into the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. Pottery from the site traces a trade network reaching as far as Southeast Asia.
properties.image_credit: Arikamedu archaeological site, a Roman-era trading settlement on India's Coromandel coast · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Anuradhapura
properties.one_line: A freedman of the Roman tax collector Annius Plocamus was blown off course and landed in Sri Lanka around 45 CE, and the curious king sent four ambassadors back to Rome with him. They spent months reaching Emperor Claudius and described their island's customs to Pliny the Elder, who recorded it as Rome's fullest account of Taprobane. The mission marked the first direct diplomatic contact between Rome and Sri Lanka.
properties.image_credit: Ruwanwelisaya stupa at Anuradhapura, capital of the Sinhalese king who sent envoys to Claudius · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Petra
properties.one_line: Nabataean kings ruled from Petra as Roman clients for over a century, paying tribute after Pompey's general Aemilius Scaurus besieged the city in 62 BCE and Aretas III bought him off with 300 talents of silver. That relationship held through decades of diplomacy until Trajan annexed the kingdom outright in 106 CE, absorbing it as the province of Arabia. Petra's rock-cut Treasury facade still stands as the monument of that vanished independent kingdom.
properties.image_credit: Al-Khazneh, the Treasury facade at Petra, capital of the Nabataean kingdom · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Panticapaeum
properties.one_line: The Bosporan Kingdom on the Crimean peninsula became a Roman client state in 63 CE and kept its own line of kings for nearly four centuries under Roman oversight. Its capital, Panticapaeum, minted coins stamped with both its own rulers and the reigning Roman emperor. Roman garrison troops, including Thracian and Cypriot cohorts, were stationed there to secure the Black Sea's northern approach.
properties.image_credit: Ruins of Panticapaeum, capital of the Roman client Bosporan Kingdom · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Two British kings, Dumnobellaunus and Tincomarus, fled to Rome as suppliants around 7 CE after losing their thrones at home, and Augustus named them among the foreign rulers who sought his protection in his Res Gestae. Their arrival let Augustus claim influence over Britain decades before Claudius's actual conquest in 43 CE. Neither man is known to have returned home to rule again.
properties.image_credit: The Ara Pacis in Rome, an Augustan monument from the era the British kings sought refuge there · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Fishbourne
properties.one_line: Rome installed Togidubnus as a client king over several southern British territories after the invasion of 43 CE, and the historian Tacitus recorded that he stayed loyal down to his own time, around 98 CE. His likely residence at Fishbourne grew into a palace of more than 100 rooms with early mosaic floors, the largest Roman residence known north of the Alps. The palace remained in use into the 2nd century CE.
properties.image_credit: Cupid on a Dolphin mosaic floor at Fishbourne Roman Palace · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Kottayam
properties.one_line: Villagers near Kottayam in Kerala unearthed a brass vessel packed with Roman gold coins in 1847, a hoard so large that witnesses described it as five porters' loads, close to 8,000 aurei. Local jewelers melted most of it down before officials could intervene, but 74 surviving coins reached museum collections in Madras and Kolkata. The find is one of dozens of Roman coin hoards recovered across southern India, physical proof of centuries of direct trade.
properties.image_credit: Roman gold coins from a southern Indian hoard (representative image, not the Kottayam coins themselves) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Zeugma
properties.one_line: Roman governor Lucius Vitellius met Parthian king Artabanus II on a bridge over the Euphrates in 37 CE, each walking to the middle with his own bodyguard. Artabanus sacrificed to the Roman standards and sent his son Darius to Rome as a hostage, along with a seven-cubit-tall Jewish giant named Eleazar as a gift. The meeting secured peace on the eastern frontier for the rest of Tiberius's reign.
properties.image_credit: Mosaic from Zeugma, the Roman frontier city near the Euphrates bridge where Vitellius met Artabanus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Darius, son of the Parthian king Artabanus II, arrived in Rome as a hostage in 37 CE after his father's peace meeting with the Roman governor Vitellius on the Euphrates. He lived on in the city for years afterward, recorded only once more riding in Caligula's entourage across the emperor's bridge of boats at Baiae. His presence in Rome stood as a guarantee of Parthian good faith won without a single battle.
properties.image_credit: The Roman Forum, Rome, where foreign hostage princes lived under the emperor's watch · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Adulis
properties.one_line: Roman merchants sailed to the Red Sea port of Adulis to trade with King Zoscales of Aksum, exchanging glassware, wine, and fine textiles for ivory, incense, and gold. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, written around 40 to 70 CE, named Zoscales the sole ruler over that stretch of coast and described him as stingy in trade but versed in Greek letters. Excavations at Adulis later uncovered Roman amphorae and glass vessels among the port's ruins, confirming steady contact with Roman markets. Ivory that once flowed north to Meroe was rerouted through Adulis instead, giving Aksum control over a key artery of Rome's African trade.

properties.name: Zafar (Saphar)
properties.one_line: Himyarite king Charibael ruled the Homerite and Sabaean peoples from his capital at Saphar and kept peace with Rome through continual embassies and gifts sent to the emperors. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, compiled around 40 to 70 CE, named him a personal friend of the emperors and praised his goodwill toward Greek traders passing through his territory. His control over the incense-rich South Arabian coast let Roman merchants sail on toward India by way of ports like Muza under his protection. That protected route carried frankincense and myrrh north into the Roman economy for generations.

properties.name: Begram
properties.one_line: Kushan rulers stored Roman bronze statuettes and glassware from Roman Egypt inside two sealed treasure rooms at their summer capital of Begram. French archaeologists opened the vaults in 1937 and found the remains of about 180 pieces of Roman glass packed alongside Chinese lacquer bowls and Indian ivory carvings. The mixed hoard showed Kushan territory sitting astride Silk Road traffic that linked Rome, India, and Han China all at once. The vaults were sealed during the 1st or 2nd century CE, preserving the clearest single snapshot of goods moving between Rome and the Kushan realm.

properties.name: Meroe
properties.one_line: Kushite queen Amanirenas fought Rome to a standstill after her armies sacked Roman towns in Upper Egypt and tore down statues of Augustus at Syene around 25 BCE. Envoys from Meroe met Augustus on the island of Samos in 21 BCE and struck a peace treaty that fixed the frontier and freed Kush from tribute for the next three centuries. Kushite soldiers had carried one captured bronze head of Augustus home in triumph and buried the 46-centimeter head beneath the steps of Meroe's temple of Amun, so worshippers trod on the emperor's face for generations. Archaeologists excavated the buried head in 1910, and it is now displayed in the British Museum.
properties.province: Kingdom of Kush (outside the Roman Empire)

properties.name: Armazi (Harmozica)
properties.one_line: Roman emperor Vespasian paid to rebuild the fortress walls of Harmozica for King Mithridates I of Iberia in 75 CE, shoring up a Caucasus ally against raids by the Alans. A bilingual Aramaic and Greek inscription set up at the site called Mithridates 'friend of the Caesars' and king of the Rome-loving Iberians. The alliance gave Rome a foothold on the far side of the Caucasus without stationing a single legion there. Iberia remained a steady Roman client along that frontier for decades afterward, continuing into Hadrian's reign.
properties.image_credit: Mtskheta, capital of the ancient Kingdom of Iberia (cathedral site postdates 117 CE) · Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as neighbor_kingdom_of_iberia)

properties.name: Ctesiphon
properties.one_line: Trajan crowned the Parthian noble Parthamaspates as Rome's client king of Parthia outside Ctesiphon in 116 CE, choosing a puppet ruler over outright annexation of the Parthian heartland. Cassius Dio described Parthamaspates performing proskynesis before Trajan as Roman troops looked on, a scene later stamped onto a Roman sestertius reading REX PARTHIS DATUS. It was the only time in Roman history an emperor personally installed a king over the whole Parthian empire. The arrangement collapsed within a year, once the rival claimant Osroes reclaimed the throne after Rome's legions withdrew.
properties.image_credit: 1864 photograph of the ancient ruins near Ctesiphon, Wikimedia Commons, public domain (reused, same site as substrate_mesopotamian_ctesiphon)

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Italicus, nephew of the German war leader Arminius, grew up in Rome as a ward of the imperial household, trained in horsemanship by both German and Roman methods. In 47 CE the Cherusci sent envoys asking Claudius to release him as their new king after years of civil war had wiped out their native nobility. Tacitus recorded that Italicus arrived among his father's people looking and speaking like a Roman, and was welcomed at first as a symbol of restored order. His reign proved short-lived once rival nobles turned against a king they judged too Roman to lead them.

properties.name: Artaxata
properties.one_line: Germanicus crowned the Pontic prince Zeno as king of Armenia at Artaxata in 18 CE, with the assembled Armenian nobility and crowds looking on as he took the throne name Artaxias III. Zeno had grown up admiring Armenian customs and language, which Tacitus wrote won him greater favor than any purely Roman candidate could have earned. Rome and Parthia had fought for years over who controlled the Armenian throne, and this joint coronation briefly settled the question without a battle. Artaxias III ruled for sixteen years until his death in 34 CE, after which the throne again became a flashpoint between Rome and Parthia.
properties.image_credit: The Ararat plain near Artaxata, Armenia's ancient capital (monastery postdates 117 CE) · Wikimedia Commons (reused, same site as neighbor_armenia_117)

properties.name: Karur
properties.one_line: Karur served as the inland capital of the Tamil Chera kings, where Roman gold and silver coins arrived by the hundreds along caravan routes from the western coast. Museum excavations there in 1973, 1977, and 1993 recovered Roman coin hoards alongside Arretine tableware and amphora sherds bearing Roman potters' stamps. Roman traders exchanged wine and Mediterranean glassware for pepper, gemstones, and pearls funneled through Chera territory. The finds mark Karur as a major inland node in the same Indo-Roman trade network that ran through the coastal port of Muziris.

properties.name: Ravenna
properties.one_line: Maroboduus built the first great confederation of Germanic tribes as king of the Marcomanni, ruling from a fortified base in Bohemia for nearly two decades. Rival nobles drove him out in 18 CE, and when he appealed to Emperor Tiberius for aid, Rome answered by granting him refuge rather than an army. He settled at Ravenna as a guest under Roman oversight, still addressed as king but stripped of any kingdom to rule. Maroboduus spent his final eighteen years there and died in 37 CE, never returning to Germania.
properties.image_credit: Fragment of Ravenna's Roman-era Porta Aurea (built 42 CE) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Hoq Cave
properties.one_line: Greek and Palmyrene sailors carved their names into the walls of Hoq Cave on the remote island the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea called Dioscorida, alongside travelers writing in Indian, South Arabian, and Aksumite scripts. Close to 250 inscriptions and drawings survive there, left by merchants who stopped at the island while sailing the monsoon route between Roman Egypt, South Arabia, and India. The Periplus described the island's inhabitants as subjects of the incense-land king across the strait, who leased its harbor out to foreign traders. Socotra's position astride the entrance to the Gulf of Aden made it a routine waypoint for Roman-era shipping bound for the Indian Ocean.

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Dacian king Decebalus sent his brother Diegis to Rome in 89 CE to seal a peace treaty ending years of war along the Danube frontier. Emperor Domitian placed a diadem on Diegis's head in a public ceremony, a symbolic act asserting that Rome alone held the right to grant Dacia's kingship. In return Domitian promised Decebalus an annual subsidy of eight million sesterces and sent Roman engineers to help fortify his kingdom. The uneasy peace held until Trajan invaded Dacia in 101 CE and annexed it outright by 106.
